## Why NVDA and Student-t?

NVIDIA (NVDA) is an ideal testing ground for heavy-tailed volatility models. As documented by Cont (2001), a fundamental "stylized fact" across financial markets is the presence of heavy tails and extreme fluctuations. In the statistical analysis of highly volatile assets, these extreme fluctuations manifest as jump risks—heavy-tailed deviations and extreme outliers that Gaussian assumptions fail to capture.

Traditional financial models typically assume returns follow a normal distribution, which severely underestimates the probability of extreme events. To capture NVDA's inherent extreme market movements, we adopt a Student-t likelihood. However, from a statistical computing perspective, the posterior distribution of a Student-t model with unknown degrees of freedom is non-standard and lacks a closed-form solution. This absence of a conjugate prior naturally motivates our use of Bayesian inference via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods.

## Preliminary EDA Findings

Using daily log returns from 2024-01-02 to 2026-09-30 (N = 688), the annualized sample standard deviation is approximately 47.8%, confirming NVDA's status as a highly volatile, high-risk tech stock. The sample kurtosis is 7.72, far above the normal benchmark of 3. The most extreme daily loss and gain in this period were -18.6% and +17.2%, respectively. These severe outliers serve as direct empirical evidence of the extreme jump risks within the dataset.

The histogram (Figure 1) shows that a fitted normal curve underestimates density near the mode and severely underestimates density in both tails. The Q-Q plot (Figure 2) confirms a systematic departure from normality. The distinct S-shape in the Q-Q plot clearly indicates a leptokurtic distribution, consistent with NVDA's highly volatile nature. The sample skewness is -0.09, indicating near symmetry.

## Methodology Preview and Literature Context

The Student-t distribution is the simplest formalization of heavy tails (e.g., Fama, 1965; Bollerslev, 1987), acting as a robust statistical proxy for jump-induced outliers. To estimate the parameters of this Student-t model, we will implement a custom Random Walk Metropolis (RWM) algorithm. Because the scale parameter \(\sigma\) and degrees of freedom \(\nu\) are constrained (e.g., \(\nu > 2\)), we will apply unconstrained transformations (e.g., \(\ln\sigma\) and \(\ln(\nu-2)\)) and include Jacobian corrections in the log-posterior density.

Furthermore, to ensure the reliability of our Bayesian estimates, we will generate three independent MCMC chains with overdispersed initial values. We will evaluate convergence using Trace plots, the Gelman-Rubin \(\hat{R}\) statistic, and Effective Sample Size (ESS), following the diagnostic frameworks covered in class. Ultimately, this MCMC implementation will allow us to conduct a comparative risk analysis, demonstrating how the Student-t model provides more realistic risk bounds than the Normal model during extreme market downturns.
